ABNB: Runs a marketplace for short-term home rentals and experiences, taking a percentage service fee from both guest and host on each booking; hosts, not Airbnb, own the properties.
ABSI: Uses generative AI plus wet-lab screening to design antibodies; revenue comes from upfront and milestone payments under biopharma partnerships such as Almirall, with lead candidate ABS-201 in early trials for hair loss.
ACHR: Developing the Midnight electric vertical-takeoff aircraft for short urban and regional hops, with order commitments from United Airlines and Gulf operators plus a defence variant; still essentially pre-revenue.
ADPT: Sells clonoSEQ, an FDA-cleared sequencing test for measurable residual disease in blood cancers reimbursed by insurers, plus immunoSEQ research services and immune-receptor data partnerships with drugmakers.
ADSK: Sells subscription design software: AutoCAD, Revit and Autodesk Construction Cloud to architects, engineers and builders; Inventor and Fusion to manufacturers; Maya and 3ds Max to film, games and VFX studios.
ALGN: Sells Invisalign clear aligners through dentists and orthodontists, along with the iTero intraoral scanners and exocad CAD/CAM software that drive the digital treatment planning workflow.
ALMR: Sells the ARGO HT automated proteomics instrument and NULISA immunoassay panels that detect very low-abundance blood proteins, to pharma and academic research labs, particularly for Alzheimer's and neurology biomarkers.
AMD: Sells x86 CPUs (Ryzen, EPYC), gaming and Instinct data-centre GPUs, and Xilinx FPGAs and adaptive SoCs to PC makers, cloud operators, game-console vendors and embedded/industrial customers.
AME: Sells electronic instruments and electromechanical devices: aircraft and process sensors, power and test instrumentation, precision motion components, and engineered materials, mostly to aerospace, energy and industrial OEMs.
AMZN: Sells goods through its own online retail and third-party marketplace (taking seller fees), rents cloud computing via AWS, sells advertising placements, and collects Prime subscription fees.
ARCT: Clinical-stage mRNA developer; earns royalties and milestones from Kostaive, a self-amplifying mRNA COVID vaccine partnered with CSL, while developing inhaled ARCT-032 for cystic fibrosis and ARCT-810 for OTC deficiency.
ATAI: Clinical-stage psychedelic drug developer with no product revenue; lead asset BPL-003 is an intranasal mebufotenin (5-MeO-DMT) formulation in late-stage trials for treatment-resistant depression, alongside earlier candidates for anxiety and cognitive impairment.
ATI: Melts and processes titanium, nickel superalloys and specialty steels into forgings, plate, sheet and precision components for jet engines, airframes, defence and medical implant customers.
AUR: Building the Aurora Driver self-driving software and sensor stack for long-haul freight trucks, now running driverless Texas lanes; charges shippers and carriers per mile rather than selling trucks.
AVAV: Sells small reconnaissance drones such as Puma and JUMP 20 and Switchblade loitering munitions to the US Army and allied militaries, and since acquiring BlueHalo also directed-energy, counter-drone and space systems.
AVGO: Sells custom AI accelerators and networking switch/PHY chips to hyperscalers, plus wireless components for iPhones, broadband and storage silicon, and licenses infrastructure software including VMware, CA and Symantec.
AVNT: Compounds and sells specialised polymer materials: colour and additive masterbatches, engineered thermoplastic compounds, and composites including Dyneema high-strength fibre used in body armour and ropes.
BABA: Runs Taobao and Tmall, where merchants pay for listings, ads and commissions; also operates Alibaba.com and AliExpress for cross-border trade, Cainiao logistics, and Alibaba Cloud, China's largest cloud provider.
BEAM: Clinical-stage biotech developing base-editing medicines such as BEAM-101 for sickle cell disease and BEAM-302 for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; no approved products, revenue comes from pharma collaborations.
BFLY: Sells the Butterfly iQ handheld ultrasound probe, which uses a semiconductor chip instead of piezoelectric crystals, plus software subscriptions, to hospitals, clinics and medical schools.
BIDU: China's largest search engine, monetised through search and feed advertising; also sells Baidu AI Cloud services and ERNIE model access, and runs the Apollo Go robotaxi service.
BLSH: Operates a regulated digital-asset exchange for institutions, earning fees and spreads on spot and options trading in crypto, and owns the CoinDesk media, indices and events business.
BMNR: Holds a large Ethereum treasury funded by share issuance and earns staking yield on it, while providing bitcoin mining advisory, hosting and equipment-leasing services as it winds down self-mining.
BWXT: Manufactures naval nuclear reactors and fuel for US Navy submarines and carriers, and supplies nuclear components, fuel handling, medical isotopes and microreactor work to government and utility customers.
CAT: Builds and sells excavators, bulldozers, mining trucks, and diesel and gas engines and generator sets, plus aftermarket parts and service, to construction firms, miners and energy operators through dealers, and finances purchases via Cat Financial.
CBRS: Sells wafer-scale AI processors and the CS-series systems built around them, plus cloud inference capacity, to AI labs and governments; revenue has been heavily concentrated in UAE customers.
CCJ: Mines and mills uranium at Cigar Lake and McArthur River in Saskatchewan and sells U3O8 under long-term contracts to nuclear utilities; also converts uranium and, via Westinghouse, sells reactor services.
CDNA: Sells transplant-monitoring lab tests to hospitals and nephrologists, chiefly AlloSure donor-derived cell-free DNA and AlloMap gene expression for detecting organ rejection, alongside transplant patient software and lab reagents.
CERS: Sells the INTERCEPT Blood System to blood banks: single-use kits and illuminator devices that use amotosalen and UV light to inactivate viruses and bacteria in donated platelets and plasma.
CMPS: Clinical-stage drug developer with no approved product, testing COMP360, a synthetic psilocybin administered with psychological support, for treatment-resistant depression and PTSD.
CNTN: Holds and stakes Canton Coin as a treasury asset and runs a Super Validator node on the Canton blockchain network, earning validator and locking-as-a-service fees; it sold its Gravitas Life Sciences biotech unit in 2026.
COIN: Runs a crypto exchange, earning trading commissions from retail and institutional users, plus custody fees, staking rewards, interest shared on USDC reserves, and subscription revenue from Coinbase One.
CRCL: Issues the USDC and EURC stablecoins and earns almost all its revenue from interest on the cash and Treasuries backing them, sharing much of it with distribution partners such as Coinbase.
CRS: Melts and finishes specialty alloys and stainless steels, mostly nickel and cobalt superalloys and titanium sold as bar, billet and wire into jet engine and aerostructure parts, plus medical and energy applications.
CRSP: Clinical-stage gene editor whose only marketed product is Casgevy, a CRISPR sickle-cell and beta-thalassemia therapy sold with Vertex; other revenue is collaboration and milestone payments from partners.
CRWD: Sells the Falcon security platform as per-endpoint subscriptions to enterprises and governments, covering endpoint detection, identity protection, cloud security and log/SIEM modules, plus breach investigation services.
CRWV: Rents GPU compute capacity in its own data centres under multi-year contracts to AI labs and hyperscalers, providing the clusters, storage and orchestration software for training and inference.
DASH: Runs a delivery marketplace for restaurants, groceries and retail, taking commissions from merchants plus consumer delivery fees, DashPass subscriptions and advertising, and owns Wolt in Europe.
DDD: Sells industrial 3D printers using stereolithography, selective laser sintering and metal powder-bed fusion, plus the resins and powders that feed them, to aerospace, industrial and dental/medical device customers.
DDOG: Sells cloud observability software on usage-based subscriptions, letting engineering teams monitor infrastructure, trace application performance, search logs and run security monitoring across their cloud estates.
DE: Sells tractors, combines and sprayers to farmers, construction and forestry machinery to contractors, and precision-agriculture guidance and telematics subscriptions, financing much of it through John Deere Financial.
DKNG: Takes bets through its online sportsbook and runs iGaming casino apps in US states where legal, earning the hold on wagers plus advertising; also owns Golden Nugget Online and DraftKings DFS contests.
ESLT: Israeli defence contractor selling drones, electro-optics and night vision, artillery and mortar systems, missiles, avionics and helmet-mounted displays to Israel's military and foreign armed forces, mostly via export contracts.
ETOR: Retail trading platform offering stocks, ETFs, crypto and CFDs with CopyTrader social features; earns most of its money from spreads on crypto and CFD trades plus interest on customer cash balances.
FIG: Sells subscription seats to its browser-based interface design and prototyping tool, plus FigJam whiteboarding, Dev Mode and Figma Slides, bought mainly by product designers, engineers and marketers inside companies.
FUTU: Runs the Futubull and moomoo online brokerage apps for retail investors in Hong Kong, Singapore, the US and Japan; revenue comes from trading commissions, margin financing and idle-cash interest, fund distribution and IPO underwriting.
GE: Designs, builds and services jet engines under the GE Aerospace name, including the CFM LEAP and GEnx for airliners and military engines, with most profit coming from spare parts and long-term maintenance contracts.
GENB: Clinical-stage drug developer using generative AI protein design; lead candidate GB-0895 is a long-acting anti-TSLP antibody in Phase 3 for severe asthma. Current cash comes from partnerships with Amgen and Novartis, not product sales.
GENI: Buys exclusive official data rights from leagues (NFL, FIBA, English Football League) and resells live data feeds, odds and trading services to sportsbooks, plus streaming and advertising technology to leagues and teams.
GH: Sells blood-based cancer tests billed to insurers: Guardant360 for tumour genotyping in advanced cancer, Reveal for residual disease, and Shield for colorectal cancer screening, plus data services to drugmakers.
GOOG: Sells search and YouTube advertising, rents computing and AI models through Google Cloud, takes a commission on Play Store apps, and sells Pixel hardware and Workspace subscriptions.
GOOGL: Makes most of its money from Google Search and YouTube advertising, plus Google Cloud infrastructure and Workspace subscriptions, Play Store commissions, Pixel hardware, and YouTube/Google One subscriptions.
GRMN: Makes GPS-enabled hardware: fitness and outdoor smartwatches, inReach satellite messengers, marine chartplotters and sonar, certified aviation avionics, and automotive OEM infotainment systems, sold to consumers, boat builders and carmakers.
GTLB: Sells subscription tiers of its DevOps platform - Git repository hosting, CI/CD pipelines, code security scanning and Duo AI assistance - to enterprise engineering teams, as SaaS or self-managed installs.
HEI: Manufactures FAA-approved PMA replacement parts and repairs for jet engines and aircraft as cheaper alternatives to OEM parts, sold to airlines and MROs; a second segment makes niche electronic components for defence, space and medical gear.
HONA: Sells business-jet and helicopter engines, auxiliary power units, avionics and flight decks, wheels and brakes, and satellite connectivity to airlines, aircraft makers and militaries; a majority of profit comes from high-margin aftermarket spares and repairs.
HOOD: Commission-free brokerage for retail investors that makes money from routing order flow to market makers, crypto trading spreads, margin and securities lending, interest on cash, and Gold subscriptions.
HPQ: Sells Windows PCs, laptops and workstations to consumers and businesses, plus laser and inkjet printers, and earns high-margin recurring revenue from ink, toner and 3D printing supplies.
ILMN: Sells DNA sequencing instruments such as the NovaSeq X to research labs, hospitals and biopharma, and earns most of its margin on the reagent kits and flow cells those machines consume.
IONS: Develops antisense RNA drugs; sells Tryngolza and Wainua directly and collects royalties and milestones on partnered drugs such as Spinraza from Biogen and Qalsody.
IRDM: Operates a 66-satellite low-earth-orbit constellation and sells voice, narrowband data and IoT airtime through partners to maritime, aviation and government users, including a large fixed-price US Department of Defense contract.
ISRG: Sells da Vinci surgical robots and Ion lung biopsy systems to hospitals, but earns most revenue from the single-use instruments and endoscopes consumed each procedure plus service contracts.
JBL: Contract manufacturer that builds electronics and mechanical assemblies for other companies' brands, from AI data centre server racks and networking gear to medical devices, car electronics and phone components, earning thin margins on huge volume.
JOBY: Developing an electric vertical-takeoff air taxi for short urban trips. Pre-revenue on aircraft; current income comes from a US Air Force contract and early Dubai/US commercial service preparation.
KALU: Rolls, extrudes and forges semi-finished aluminium products such as plate, sheet, extrusions and rod, sold to aerospace and defence primes, automotive suppliers, packaging converters and general engineering customers.
KDK: Sells the Kodiak Driver self-driving system for heavy trucks, charging per-mile driver-as-a-service fees to freight carriers and selling driverless trucks to oilfield operators such as Atlas Energy in the Permian Basin.
KLAR: Provides buy-now-pay-later checkout financing; earns fees from merchants per transaction, interest and late fees from consumers on longer-term instalment loans, plus advertising revenue in its shopping app and interchange on the Klarna card.
KMT: Makes tungsten carbide cutting tools, indexable inserts, drills and end mills for metal machining, plus wear-resistant parts and earthworking tips, sold to aerospace, automotive, energy and general machine shops.
KSPI: Kazakhstan super-app combining card payments and merchant acquiring, consumer BNPL and deposit-funded lending, and an e-commerce marketplace with delivery; also owns Turkish online retailer Hepsiburada.
KTOS: Sells low-cost jet-powered drones and target drones, small turbine engines, hypersonic and rocket test vehicles, satellite ground systems and microwave electronics, mostly to the US military and allied governments.
LECO: Makes arc welding equipment, welding consumables such as stick electrodes and flux-cored wire, plasma cutting systems and welding automation and robotic cells, sold to shipyards, pipeline builders and general fabricators.
LHX: Supplies defence electronics to the US and allied militaries: tactical radios, night-vision and targeting optics, electronic warfare, space sensors and satellites, and Aerojet Rocketdyne solid rocket motors and missiles.
LLY: Makes and sells prescription drugs worldwide, led by the GLP-1 medicines Mounjaro and Zepbound for diabetes and obesity, plus Verzenio, Jardiance, Taltz and the Alzheimer's antibody Kisunla.
LMT: Sells F-35 and F-16 fighter jets and C-130 transports, missiles and fire control systems (PAC-3, HIMARS, JASSM, Javelin), Sikorsky helicopters, and satellites and Trident missiles, almost entirely to the US government and allied militaries.
LUNR: Builds and flies Nova-C lunar landers under NASA CLPS delivery contracts, and sells lunar communications relay satellites, orbital services and engineering support to NASA and defence agencies.
MASS: Sells handheld analytical instruments to military units, bomb squads, police and customs agencies, principally the MX908 mass spectrometer and XplorIR Raman analyser for identifying fentanyl, explosives and chemical warfare agents, plus consumables and service.
MELI: Runs Latin America's largest online marketplace, earning commissions from third-party sellers plus fees from Mercado Pago payments and credit, Mercado Envios logistics, and advertising sold to merchants.
META: Sells targeted advertising on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads, which is nearly all its revenue; Reality Labs sells Quest headsets and Ray-Ban smart glasses at a loss.
MMM: Sells adhesives, tapes, abrasives, films and coatings across industrial, automotive and electronics markets, plus consumer brands such as Post-it, Scotch tape and Command hooks, and personal safety gear like respirators.
MOG.A: Makes precision motion control hardware: hydraulic and electric flight control actuators for commercial and military aircraft, missile steering and space vehicle actuation systems, plus industrial servo valves and controls.
MTLS: Runs a large contract 3D printing bureau for industrial and medical parts, and licenses software including Magics build-preparation and Mimics medical image segmentation used to design patient-specific implants and surgical guides.
MTRN: Supplies advanced materials: beryllium and beryllium-copper alloys, precision optical coatings and thin-film targets, and specialty inorganic chemicals, sold into semiconductor, defence, aerospace and medical imaging markets.
NET: Sells subscription network services routed through its global edge network: CDN and DDoS protection, zero-trust access, WAF and bot management, DNS, and Workers serverless compute, mostly to businesses.
NFLX: Sells monthly streaming subscriptions for its licensed and original films and series in over 190 countries, and increasingly sells advertising on its cheaper ad-supported tier; also expanding into games and live events.
NNDM: Sells industrial additive manufacturing and electronics production equipment to defence, aerospace and medical device makers, including DragonFly printed-electronics printers, Essemtec SMT pick-and-place lines, GIS inkjet systems and metal binder jetting machines.
NRIX: Clinical-stage biotech developing targeted protein degraders and CBL-B inhibitors for blood cancers. Revenue today is milestone and research payments from Gilead and Sanofi partnerships, not product sales.
NTLA: Clinical-stage biotech developing in-vivo CRISPR therapies, chiefly lonvo-z for hereditary angioedema (BLA filing under way) and nex-z for ATTR amyloidosis; no approved products or product revenue yet.
NTRA: Runs cell-free DNA lab tests billed to insurers and Medicare: Panorama prenatal screening, Signatera for detecting residual cancer after treatment, and Prospera for organ-transplant rejection.
NU: Digital bank serving Brazil, Mexico and Colombia; makes money from credit card interest and interchange, personal loans, deposit spreads, insurance and investment products sold through its app to roughly 100 million retail customers.
NVDA: Sells data-centre GPUs and networking systems for AI training and inference, GeForce gaming cards, and automotive chips, with the CUDA software stack keeping developers on its hardware.
OKLO: Pre-revenue developer of small sodium-cooled fast fission reactors (the Aurora powerhouse); plans to own the plants and sell electricity and heat under long-term power purchase agreements to data centres and defence sites, plus used-fuel recycling.
P: Formerly Pure Storage, renamed Everpure in 2026. Sells all-flash enterprise storage arrays (FlashArray, FlashBlade) with Purity software, plus Evergreen subscription capacity and Portworx container storage, to enterprises and cloud operators.
PACB: Sells DNA sequencing instruments and the consumable reagent kits and SMRT Cells they consume, chiefly the long-read Revio and short-read Onso systems, to research labs and genome centres.
PAYP: Operates Japan's dominant QR-code mobile payments app with roughly 72 million users; earns merchant transaction fees and revenue from adjacent consumer credit cards, BNPL, banking, securities brokerage and in-app advertising.
PLTR: Sells Gotham and Foundry data-integration and analytics software, plus the AIP model layer, to US and allied defence and intelligence agencies and to large corporates, usually with paid deployment engineers.
PONY: Chinese autonomous driving firm operating paid robotaxi fleets in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen, plus driverless trucking; earns ride fares, licensing fees and technology contracts with automakers.
PRLB: Takes uploaded CAD files and quotes and manufactures low-volume custom parts by CNC machining, injection moulding, sheet metal fabrication and 3D printing, selling prototypes and short production runs to product engineers.
PRME: Preclinical and early-clinical gene editing company developing prime editing therapies, lead programs in Wilson's disease and cystic fibrosis. No product revenue; funded by collaborations and capital raises.
PSNL: Sells NeXT Personal, a tumour-informed blood test that detects residual and recurrent cancer, to oncologists under Medicare coverage, and runs sequencing and biomarker services for pharma clinical trials.
PTC: Sells subscription engineering software to industrial manufacturers: Creo CAD, Windchill product lifecycle management, Codebeamer requirements and software lifecycle tools, Onshape cloud CAD and ThingWorx industrial IoT.
QSI: Sells the Platinum benchtop single-molecule protein sequencer to academic and pharmaceutical proteomics labs, plus the recurring semiconductor chips, reagent kits and service contracts each instrument consumes.
RBLX: Runs a free user-generated 3D game platform and makes money selling Robux virtual currency to players, keeping most of it while paying creators a share, plus in-game advertising.
RBRK: Sells subscription software that backs up and recovers enterprise data across data centres, SaaS apps and cloud, with immutable snapshots and ransomware detection aimed at recovery after attacks.
RKLB: Launches small satellites on its Electron rocket and hypersonic test payloads on HASTE while developing the larger Neutron, and sells satellite buses and components such as solar arrays and reaction wheels to defence and commercial operators.
ROKU: Sells low-cost streaming players and licenses Roku OS to TV makers, then monetises the resulting user base through advertising, subscription revenue shares and placement fees from streaming services.
RXRX: Runs automated wet labs and machine-learning models to identify drug candidates; income comes from pharma collaborations with Roche/Genentech and Bayer plus its own clinical pipeline, not from marketed medicines.
SCTX: Clinical-stage gene editing company engineering compact CasX CRISPR enzymes into in vivo genetic medicines, starting with cardiometabolic disease; pre-product revenue, funded by IPO proceeds and collaborations with Sanofi and other pharma partners.
SDGR: Licenses physics-based molecular simulation software to pharma and materials companies, and runs its own drug discovery programs, earning software subscriptions plus milestones and equity stakes in partnered biotechs.
SE: Runs Shopee, Southeast Asia's largest e-commerce marketplace (commissions, ads, logistics fees), the Garena games business built on Free Fire, and Monee, a digital lending and payments arm; also operates in Brazil.
SECZ: SEC-registered tokenization platform that issues, records and administers tokenized funds and securities on public blockchains, acting as transfer agent and broker-dealer for products such as BlackRock's BUIDL fund and earning fees on assets under administration.
SHOP: Sells subscription e-commerce software that lets merchants run online and retail stores, then takes a cut of their sales through Shopify Payments, shipping, POS hardware, lending and app-store fees.
SNOW: Sells a cloud data warehouse and analytics platform on consumption pricing, charging enterprises per second of compute and per terabyte stored to query, share and build applications on their data.
SNPS: Licenses EDA software used to design and verify chips, sells reusable semiconductor IP blocks, and since the Ansys deal sells physics simulation tools, to chipmakers and electronics firms on multi-year subscriptions.
SOFI: Digital bank offering personal, student and mortgage loans, deposit accounts, credit cards and brokerage to consumers, and separately licenses Galileo card-issuing and core banking software to other fintechs.
SPCX: Sells rocket launch services on Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy and Starship to NASA, the Pentagon and commercial satellite operators, and Starlink satellite broadband subscriptions to consumers, aviation, maritime and government users.
SPOT: Sells ad-free Premium music and podcast subscriptions to consumers and sells advertising against its free tier, paying most of the resulting revenue back to record labels and publishers as royalties.
SRTA: Provides time-critical medical logistics: air and ground transport of donor organs and transplant teams, organ recovery and preservation services, plus cardiac perfusion, ECMO and autotransfusion staffing for hospitals.
SSYS: Sells polymer 3D printers to manufacturers and designers, mainly FDM and PolyJet machines, and makes much of its money on the proprietary filament, resin and photopolymer materials those printers consume.
SYM: Builds robotic warehouse automation systems - mobile bots, storage structures and control software - installed in distribution centres, sold largely to Walmart and other grocery and retail chains under multi-year deployment contracts.
TDY: Sells digital imaging sensors and cameras (infrared, X-ray, machine vision, space), marine instruments and unmanned underwater vehicles, electronic test and measurement instruments, and defence electronics to industrial, government and aerospace customers.
TEM: Sells genomic sequencing and molecular diagnostic tests to oncologists and hospitals, and licenses the resulting de-identified clinical and molecular data, plus AI analytics, to pharmaceutical companies.
TER: Sells automated test equipment that chipmakers and electronics manufacturers use to screen semiconductors and circuit boards, plus Universal Robots collaborative arms and MiR autonomous mobile robots for factories.
TOST: Sells restaurant point-of-sale hardware and software subscriptions, but earns most revenue from processing card payments for those restaurants, plus payroll, lending and online-ordering add-ons.
TRMB: Sells precision GPS positioning hardware and increasingly subscription software for construction layout, land surveying, agriculture guidance and trucking fleet and freight management.
TSLA: Builds and sells battery-electric cars (Model 3/Y/S/X, Cybertruck) direct to consumers, plus Megapack and Powerwall battery storage to utilities and homeowners, and paid Full Self-Driving software.
TSM: Contract chip foundry that manufactures semiconductors to order on leading-edge process nodes for fabless designers such as Apple, Nvidia, AMD and Qualcomm, plus advanced packaging services.
TWST: Manufactures synthetic DNA on a silicon chip platform, selling genes, oligo pools, NGS target-enrichment panels and antibody-discovery libraries to biotech, pharma, agriculture and academic labs.
TXG: Sells Chromium single-cell instruments and Visium/Xenium spatial-biology systems to academic and pharma research labs, with most revenue from the recurring reagent consumables those machines consume.
VCYT: Sells genomic diagnostic tests ordered by physicians and reimbursed by insurers, chiefly Afirma for indeterminate thyroid nodules, Decipher for prostate cancer risk, and Prosigna for breast cancer.
VELO: Sells laser powder-bed fusion metal 3D printers for hard-to-print parts with steep overhangs, and increasingly sells printed parts under multi-year production agreements to US defence and space customers.
WGS: Sells exome and whole-genome sequencing tests that diagnose rare genetic disease, mostly in children, ordered by hospitals and clinicians and paid for by commercial insurers and Medicaid.
WRD: Chinese developer of self-driving software running robotaxi and robobus fleets and autonomous street sweepers, selling rides, vehicles and technology services, with Uber partnerships expanding it into the Middle East and Europe.
XE: Developing the Xe-100 high-temperature gas-cooled small modular reactor and manufacturing TRISO pebble fuel; current revenue comes from US government programmes and engineering contracts with customers such as Dow and Amazon.
XMTR: Runs an online marketplace where engineers upload CAD files for instant quotes on CNC machining, 3D printing, sheet metal and injection moulded parts, routing the work to a network of contract manufacturers and taking the spread.
XRAY: Sells dental equipment and consumables to dentists, labs and distributors: CEREC chairside CAD/CAM and imaging systems, treatment centres, dental implants, SureSmile clear aligners, endodontic instruments, composites and impression materials.
XYZ: Sells card readers and merchant software to small businesses via Square, runs the Cash App consumer payments and investing app, owns the Afterpay buy-now-pay-later network, and mines bitcoin hardware.
Z: Runs the largest US residential real estate search site; sells buyer leads and advertising to agents through Premier Agent, sells rental listing advertising to landlords, and originates mortgages and title services through Zillow Home Loans.
AAPL: Sells iPhone, Mac, iPad, Watch and AirPods hardware to consumers, and takes a cut of App Store sales plus subscription fees for iCloud, Music and TV+; services now carry the margin.
MSFT: Sells Azure cloud infrastructure and Microsoft 365 and Dynamics subscriptions to enterprises, Windows licences to PC makers, and runs LinkedIn, GitHub and the Xbox business.
BRK.B: Holding company owning GEICO, BNSF Railway, Berkshire Hathaway Energy and a portfolio of manufacturing, retail and service businesses outright, funded largely by insurance float and reinvested into listed equities.
JPM: Universal bank: deposits, cards and mortgages to US consumers, lending and treasury services to corporates, plus investment banking, trading and asset management.
MU: Makes DRAM and NAND flash memory for data-centre servers, phones, PCs and cars, competing on process node and cost per bit in a market that swings hard with supply.
WMT: Runs supercentres, Sam's Club warehouses and a growing online marketplace, buying at scale and selling groceries and general merchandise on thin margins; advertising and marketplace fees are the profitable edge.
V: Operates the card network that authorises and settles transactions between banks and merchants, charging a fee per transaction and per dollar moved. It issues no cards and lends nothing.
XOM: Produces crude and natural gas, refines them into fuels, and manufactures petrochemicals; earnings track the crude price and the refining spread more than anything management does.
ASML: The only supplier of extreme-ultraviolet lithography systems, sold to TSMC, Samsung and Intel; every leading-edge chip in the world is patterned on its machines.
JNJ: Sells prescription drugs in immunology and oncology plus surgical and orthopaedic devices to hospitals; the consumer brands were spun off as Kenvue.
MA: Runs the payment network competing with Visa, charging banks and merchants per transaction to authorise and settle card payments, and sells fraud and data services on top.
CSCO: Sells switches, routers and enterprise networking gear to companies and carriers, increasingly bundled with security and observability software on subscription.
INTC: Designs and manufactures x86 CPUs for PCs and servers, and is building a contract foundry to make chips for others — the turnaround that determines whether the capital spending pays off.
ABBV: Sells Humira's successors Skyrizi and Rinvoq in immunology, plus Botox and aesthetics, oncology and neuroscience drugs, to prescribers and hospitals.
BAC: Universal bank: consumer deposits and cards, commercial lending, Merrill wealth management and an investment bank; earnings swing with the rate cycle and credit losses.
COST: Warehouse retailer that sells a deliberately narrow range at near cost and makes most of its profit from annual membership fees, which is why renewal rates matter more than sales.
AMAT: Sells deposition, etch and inspection equipment to chipmakers — the tools that build a transistor layer by layer, sold to the same handful of fabs as ASML.
CVX: Produces oil and gas, principally in the Permian and Kazakhstan, refines and markets fuels, and sells chemicals through a joint venture.
KO: Sells concentrate to independent bottlers who make and distribute Coca-Cola, Sprite, Costa and Topo Chico; the concentrate model is what keeps the margins high and the capital employed low.
UNH: Sells health insurance to employers, individuals and Medicare members, and through Optum owns the pharmacy benefit manager, clinics and physician groups that the insurance pays.
ORCL: Sells database software and ERP applications to enterprises and is spending heavily to rent GPU capacity through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, now the growth story.
LRCX: Sells etch and deposition equipment to memory and logic fabs; more exposed to memory capital spending than its peers, so it moves with the DRAM cycle.
HSBC: Universal bank concentrated in Hong Kong and the UK, earning most of its profit from Asian commercial banking and wealth management rather than from investment banking.
PG: Sells household and personal care brands — Tide, Pampers, Gillette, Head & Shoulders — through retailers, competing on brand and shelf space and passing input costs through in price.
MS: Investment bank and, increasingly, a wealth manager: advisory and trading revenue on one side, fee income from $6tn+ of client assets on the other, which is the steadier half.
HD: Sells building materials, tools and appliances through big-box stores, with professional contractors — not weekend DIY customers — accounting for roughly half of sales.
MRK: Sells Keytruda in oncology plus vaccines and animal health products; the concentration in one drug facing patent expiry is the central question for the company.
GS: Investment bank: advises on mergers, underwrites issuance, trades for institutional clients, and manages assets. Earnings are cyclical because deal volume is.
TM: Builds and sells cars worldwide under Toyota and Lexus, and runs a large captive finance arm; the hybrid line-up is its distinctive bet against a pure-electric transition.
NVS: Sells prescription drugs in cardiovascular, immunology and neuroscience, and radioligand cancer therapies; the generics business was spun off as Sandoz.
PM: Sells Marlboro outside the US plus the IQOS heated-tobacco and Zyn nicotine-pouch lines; the smoke-free products are now the growth engine and carry better margins than cigarettes.
RY: Canada's largest bank by assets: domestic retail banking and wealth management, plus capital markets and a US private bank.
RTX: Makes Pratt & Whitney jet engines, Collins avionics and Raytheon missiles and radars, selling to airframers, airlines and the Pentagon; aftermarket parts and service carry the margin.
PANW: Sells network firewalls and cloud and endpoint security software to enterprises on subscription, having pushed customers from appliances onto platform contracts.
MUFG: Japan's largest bank group: domestic lending and deposits, a trust bank, a securities arm, and large stakes in overseas banks including Morgan Stanley.
GEV: Sells gas and steam turbines, wind turbines and grid equipment to utilities — the power-generation half of the old General Electric, and the direct beneficiary of data-centre electricity demand.
AZN: Sells oncology, respiratory and cardiometabolic drugs; the pipeline in antibody-drug conjugates is what the valuation now rests on.
DELL: Sells servers, storage and PCs to enterprises and consumers, with AI server racks built around Nvidia GPUs now driving the revenue and diluting the margin.
WFC: US retail and commercial bank: deposits, mortgages, cards and commercial lending, operating under an asset cap imposed after the accounts scandal until 2025.
TXN: Makes analogue and embedded chips — power management, signal conversion, microcontrollers — sold into industrial and automotive customers, and owns its own 300mm fabs.
KLAC: Sells process-control and inspection systems that find defects on wafers; the smallest of the big three equipment makers by revenue and the most profitable by margin.
ANET: Sells high-speed data-centre switches running its own EOS software to cloud operators and large enterprises, competing directly with Cisco at the top of the network.
AXP: Issues cards, lends on them, and runs its own network, earning both the merchant discount and the interest; the annual-fee premium cards are the distinctive asset.
C: Global bank strongest in cross-border treasury services for multinationals, alongside cards and a shrinking consumer bank, mid-way through a long restructuring.
SAP: Sells ERP software that runs the finance, supply chain and HR of large enterprises, now migrating that base from on-premises licences to cloud subscriptions.
LIN: Sells industrial gases — oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, argon — to steel, chemicals, electronics and healthcare customers, usually on long take-or-pay contracts at on-site plants.
TMO: Sells lab instruments, reagents and consumables to pharma and biotech, and manufactures drugs under contract; the consumables are the recurring half.
IBM: Sells mainframes, hybrid-cloud software including Red Hat, and consulting; the software and mainframe cycle carry the profit while consulting carries the revenue.
NVO: Sells semaglutide as Ozempic for diabetes and Wegovy for obesity, plus insulins; the obesity franchise is both the growth and the entire competitive risk.
AMGN: Sells biologics in inflammation, oncology and bone health, plus a large biosimilars book and an obesity candidate in late trials.
SAN: Spanish bank whose earnings come mostly from retail lending in Brazil, Mexico, the UK and Spain rather than from its home market alone.
TD: Canadian retail bank with a large US branch network, operating under a US asset cap imposed after anti-money-laundering failures.
APH: Makes connectors, cable and interconnect systems for data centres, cars, aircraft and industrial equipment — an unglamorous component sold into almost every end market.
VZ: Sells mobile and broadband subscriptions to US consumers and businesses; a capital-heavy business competing on network quality and price, funding a large dividend.
STX: Makes hard disk drives for data-centre storage, where cost per terabyte still beats flash at scale; demand now tracks cloud capital spending rather than PCs.
MCD: Franchises restaurants and collects royalties and rent from operators rather than running most stores itself, which is why it reads more like a property and brand business than a restaurant chain.
TTE: French major producing oil and gas, refining and marketing fuels, and building one of the larger renewables and power portfolios among the oil companies.
PEP: Sells Pepsi, Gatorade and Mountain Dew alongside Frito-Lay and Quaker snacks; the snack business is larger and more profitable than the drinks.
WDC: Makes hard disk drives for data centres following the separation of its flash business as Sandisk, leaving a pure exposure to the nearline drive cycle.
TMUS: Sells mobile and home broadband subscriptions in the US, using the mid-band spectrum acquired with Sprint to compete on both coverage and price.
SCHW: Custodies retail brokerage assets and earns most of its profit on the spread between what it pays on idle client cash and what it earns investing it, rather than on trading commissions.
ABT: Sells diagnostics, medical devices including continuous glucose monitors, generic drugs in emerging markets, and infant nutrition — an unusually diversified healthcare mix.
NEE: Runs Florida Power & Light as a regulated utility and, separately, the largest US portfolio of wind and solar generation sold under long-term contracts.
SNDK: Makes NAND flash memory and SSDs, spun out of Western Digital; a pure exposure to the flash pricing cycle rather than to hard drives.
ADI: Makes high-performance analogue and mixed-signal chips — data converters, amplifiers, power — for industrial, automotive and communications customers, with long product lifetimes.
TJX: Buys branded apparel and home goods opportunistically at closeout and sells them below department-store prices through TJ Maxx, Marshalls and HomeGoods; the buying, not the stores, is the skill.
UNP: Runs the freight railroad across the western two-thirds of the US, hauling intermodal containers, coal, grain and chemicals under a duopoly with BNSF.
BA: Builds commercial airliners and defence aircraft, weapons and space systems; the commercial backlog is large and the constraint is production quality, not demand.
BUD: Brews and distributes Budweiser, Stella Artois, Corona outside the US and Michelob Ultra, with the profit concentrated in Latin America rather than in the US.
BLK: Manages roughly $12tn for institutions and individuals, mostly through iShares ETFs, and licenses the Aladdin risk system to other asset managers.
WELL: REIT owning senior housing, outpatient medical buildings and skilled nursing facilities, with the senior housing operated on profit-sharing structures rather than fixed leases.
DIS: Runs theme parks and cruise lines, ESPN and the broadcast networks, the film studios and Disney+; the parks generate the cash while streaming decides the multiple.
MRVL: Designs custom AI accelerators and the optical, ethernet and storage silicon that connects data centres, selling into a small number of very large cloud customers.
UBS: The largest global wealth manager, with an investment bank attached, still integrating Credit Suisse after the emergency takeover.
GILD: Sells HIV antivirals including the long-acting lenacapavir, plus oncology and liver disease drugs; HIV is the franchise everything else is funded from.
ETN: Sells electrical distribution and power management equipment to data centres, utilities and buildings, plus aerospace and vehicle systems — the direct beneficiary of grid and data-centre build-out.
BBVA: Spanish bank earning a large share of its profit in Mexico, where it is the market leader, alongside Spain and Turkey.
T: Sells mobile and fibre broadband subscriptions in the US, having exited media; a slower-growing, higher-yielding version of the same business as Verizon.
QCOM: Designs Snapdragon mobile processors and modems, and separately licenses its cellular patents to every handset maker — the licensing half carries most of the profit.
SCCO: Mines copper in Peru and Mexico with among the lowest costs in the industry and the longest reserve life; earnings are a levered bet on the copper price.
CRM: Sells CRM, marketing and service software to enterprises on subscription, plus the Slack and Tableau acquisitions and the Agentforce AI layer.
BKNG: Runs Booking.com, Priceline and Kayak, taking a commission on hotel and travel bookings; asset-light, so nearly all incremental revenue falls to profit.
IBKR: Runs an electronic brokerage for active and professional traders worldwide, earning commissions, margin interest and interest on client cash across 150+ markets.
COP: Independent oil and gas producer with acreage in the Permian, Alaska and Qatar LNG; no refining, so it is a purer bet on the commodity price than the majors.
UBER: Runs the ride-hailing and food delivery marketplaces, taking a cut of each trip and order, plus a freight brokerage; drivers are contractors, not employees.
PFE: Sells vaccines, oncology and internal medicine drugs; the COVID revenue has largely gone and the question is whether the Seagen oncology deal replaces it.
DHR: Sells bioprocessing consumables, diagnostics and life-science instruments to pharma manufacturers and labs, run under a well-known continuous-improvement operating system.
CB: Underwrites commercial property and casualty insurance globally, plus high-net-worth personal lines; earns from underwriting margin and from investing the float.
PLD: The largest industrial REIT, owning warehouses near major cities and ports and leasing them to retailers and logistics operators; rents reset well above expiring leases.
BMY: Sells oncology, cardiovascular and immunology drugs; several large products face patent expiry, which is what the recent acquisitions are meant to cover.
CVS: Runs the Caremark pharmacy benefit manager, the Aetna health insurer and the retail pharmacy chain — buying drugs, insuring the patients and dispensing to them inside one company.
APP: Sells an advertising engine that places ads inside mobile games and, increasingly, e-commerce apps, taking a share of the spend it converts; the ad software, not the games, is the business.
BTI: Sells Dunhill, Lucky Strike and Pall Mall cigarettes outside the US, Newport inside it, plus the Vuse vapour and Velo pouch brands.
MFG: Japanese banking group: domestic corporate lending, a securities arm and overseas wholesale banking, smaller than MUFG and more corporate-weighted.
COF: Issues credit cards and lends on cars, funded by retail deposits; more exposed to consumer credit losses than a diversified bank, and now owns Discover's network.
BMO: Canadian bank with a large US Midwest branch network acquired with Bank of the West, alongside domestic retail banking and capital markets.
PBR: Brazil's state-controlled oil company, producing from the pre-salt fields at low cost and refining domestically; policy risk on fuel pricing is part of the investment.
SYK: Sells orthopaedic implants, surgical robots and neurotechnology to hospitals, with the Mako robot placed to pull implant sales along behind it.
PGR: Underwrites US car insurance direct and through agents, competing on pricing accuracy from telematics data rather than on brand alone.
PH: Makes hydraulic, pneumatic and filtration components for industrial machinery and aircraft, with aerospace aftermarket now the most profitable part.
HDB: India's largest private bank by assets, lending to retail and corporate customers and funded by a low-cost deposit franchise.
RIO: Mines iron ore in the Pilbara, plus aluminium, copper and lithium; iron ore sold to Chinese steel mills still determines the earnings.
SPGI: Rates debt issuance, publishes the S&P index family and sells market data and commodity price assessments — three businesses with high margins and few substitutes.
VRTX: Sells the cystic fibrosis franchise it effectively monopolises, plus the Casgevy gene therapy with CRISPR Therapeutics and a non-opioid painkiller.
SBUX: Runs and franchises coffee stores worldwide, with the profit dependent on North American same-store traffic and on whether the China business recovers.
GLW: Makes specialty glass and ceramics: display glass for TVs, Gorilla Glass for phones, and optical fibre and connectivity for data centres, which is the part now growing.
ENB: Owns the pipeline network moving Canadian crude to US refineries plus a large gas utility; earnings are contracted and toll-based rather than commodity-linked.
FTNT: Sells network firewalls built on its own security chips plus SASE and security operations software, competing with Palo Alto at a lower price point.
BP: British major producing oil and gas, refining and marketing fuels, having scaled back the renewables push to concentrate on hydrocarbons and returns.
LOW: Sells building materials, appliances and garden goods through big-box stores, weighted more towards DIY customers than Home Depot and correspondingly more cyclical.
NOW: Sells workflow software that automates IT, HR and customer service processes inside large enterprises, on multi-year subscriptions with high renewal rates.
MO: Sells Marlboro inside the US, plus the NJOY vapour brand and a stake in AB InBev; volumes decline every year and price increases have so far more than covered it.
HWM: Makes jet engine components, fasteners and forged aluminium wheels for aircraft and trucks; the engine aftermarket is where the pricing power sits.
ACN: Sells IT consulting and systems integration, running large technology programmes for enterprises and governments; people, not software, are the product.
MDT: Sells cardiac devices, insulin pumps, surgical robots and neuromodulation to hospitals — the broadest device portfolio in healthcare, growing slowly.
CM: Canadian bank concentrated in domestic retail banking and mortgages, with a smaller US commercial franchise.
BNS: Canadian bank distinguished by its Latin American footprint in Mexico, Peru and Chile alongside the domestic retail business.
IBN: Indian private bank lending to retail and corporate customers, with insurance and securities subsidiaries attached.
BNY: Custodies and administers assets for institutions, settles securities and provides treasury services; a fee-and-interest business rather than a lending one.
ADP: Runs payroll and HR administration for employers, earning per-employee fees plus interest on the client tax money it holds between collection and remittance.
SO: Regulated electric utility serving Georgia and Alabama, and operator of Vogtle, the only new nuclear units built in the US this century.
SNY: Sells Dupixent in immunology plus vaccines including flu shots; Dupixent is the growth and the concentration risk at once.
BN: Owns and manages real assets — infrastructure, renewable power, real estate and private equity — earning fees on third-party capital and returns on its own.
GD: Builds nuclear submarines and combat vehicles for the Pentagon and Gulfstream business jets for corporations; the submarine backlog is effectively guaranteed volume.
MCK: Distributes prescription drugs from manufacturers to pharmacies and hospitals at very thin margins on very large volume, plus oncology practice services.
EQNR: Norwegian state-controlled producer of oil and gas, the largest supplier of pipeline gas to Europe, with an offshore wind portfolio attached.
ING: Dutch bank running a low-cost digital retail model across the Benelux, Germany and Poland, plus wholesale lending.
EQIX: REIT operating colocation data centres where networks and clouds interconnect; revenue is recurring rent plus cross-connect fees, which are the defensible part.
TT: Sells commercial HVAC systems and services to buildings and data centres, plus transport refrigeration; the service contracts are the recurring half.
PNC: US regional bank doing commercial lending, retail banking and treasury management, largely in the Midwest and mid-Atlantic.
PWR: Builds and maintains electricity transmission lines, substations and renewable projects under contract to utilities — the labour that grid expansion actually requires.
ADBE: Sells Creative Cloud, Document Cloud and marketing software on subscription; the question is whether generative image and video tools erode the creative franchise.
CNQ: Canadian producer of oil sands and conventional crude, with long-life, low-decline reserves that need little sustaining capital.
NEM: The largest gold miner, with operations across the Americas, Australia and Africa; earnings are geared to the gold price against a broadly fixed cost base.
MAR: Franchises and manages hotels under Marriott, Sheraton, Ritz-Carlton and Westin, collecting fees rather than owning the buildings.
DUK: Regulated electric and gas utility across the Carolinas, Florida, Indiana and Ohio, spending heavily on generation replacement and grid upgrades.
USB: US regional bank with retail branches, commercial lending and a large payment processing business that sets it apart from peers.
CME: Runs the futures exchanges for interest rates, equity indices, energy and agriculture, charging per contract traded and per contract cleared.
BCS: British bank pairing a domestic retail and cards business with a markets-heavy investment bank that produces most of the volatility in earnings.
BX: Manages private equity, real estate, credit and infrastructure funds for institutions, earning management fees plus a share of the gains.
CEG: The largest US operator of nuclear power stations, selling carbon-free output into wholesale markets and increasingly under long contracts to data-centre operators.
MNST: Sells energy drinks made and distributed by Coca-Cola's bottling network, which is why it earns software-like margins on a beverage.
CDNS: Sells the electronic design automation software and IP blocks chip designers use to lay out and verify silicon; a duopoly with Synopsys.
CSX: Runs the freight railroad across the eastern US, hauling intermodal, coal, chemicals and autos in a duopoly with Norfolk Southern.
VRT: Sells power and cooling systems for data centres — UPS units, busways, liquid cooling — sold directly into the AI build-out.
VLO: The largest independent US refiner, buying crude and selling gasoline, diesel and renewable diesel; earnings are the crack spread, not the oil price.
MPC: Refines crude into fuels, owns a retail network, and controls the MPLX midstream partnership; the refining margin drives the result.
RACE: Builds and sells Ferrari road cars in deliberately limited volumes, plus racing and licensing; the scarcity is what supports luxury-goods margins on a car maker.
KKR: Manages private equity, infrastructure and credit funds, and holds a large balance sheet of its own investments alongside an insurance arm.
WM: Collects and disposes of waste in North America, owning the landfills that competitors must also use, which is the source of the pricing power.
MRSH: Brokes insurance for corporate clients and sells actuarial, benefits and management consulting through Mercer and Oliver Wyman; earns commissions and fees, and carries no underwriting risk.
FCX: Mines copper in Indonesia, the US and South America, plus the gold that comes with the Grasberg ore; leveraged to the copper price with high fixed costs.
JCI: Sells building HVAC, fire safety and control systems, and the service contracts to maintain them; the installed base is what makes the service revenue recurring.
UPS: Delivers parcels in the US and internationally, running its own aircraft and vehicle fleet; a fixed-cost network where package volume and price per package decide the margin.
CMI: Makes diesel and natural gas engines for trucks and equipment, plus power generation sets for data centres, and the aftermarket parts that follow them.
WMB: Owns the Transco gas pipeline system carrying gas from the Gulf to the eastern seaboard, earning contracted fees rather than commodity margin.
E: Italian major producing oil and gas, with a large exploration record in Africa and the Mediterranean, plus refining and a retail power business.
HCA: Runs the largest US for-profit hospital network, earning on the spread between negotiated payer rates and the cost of delivering care.
INTU: Sells TurboTax and QuickBooks to consumers and small businesses, plus Credit Karma and Mailchimp; a seasonal business concentrated in the US tax filing window.
ICE: Owns the New York Stock Exchange and the energy futures markets, and sells mortgage technology and fixed-income data; exchange fees plus data subscriptions.
RCL: Operates cruise ships under Royal Caribbean, Celebrity and Silversea; a capital-intensive business where onboard spending increasingly matters as much as ticket price.
CMCSA: Runs Xfinity cable broadband, NBCUniversal and Sky, plus the theme parks; broadband generates the cash while subscriber losses set the terms of the debate.
PSX: Refines crude into fuels, owns midstream pipelines and the CPChem chemicals joint venture, and runs a retail network in Europe.
EMR: Sells process automation systems and control valves to refineries, chemical plants and life sciences manufacturers, plus the AspenTech industrial software.
MCO: Rates debt issuance and, through Moody's Analytics, sells credit data and risk software; the ratings business is a duopoly with S&P.
SHW: Makes paint and coatings, selling through its own store network to professional painters, which is the distribution advantage over competitors on retail shelves.
ITW: Makes welding equipment, industrial fasteners, food equipment and specialty components across seven segments, run to a decentralised, high-margin operating model.
EPD: Partnership owning natural gas liquids pipelines, fractionators and export terminals on the Gulf Coast, earning fees on volume rather than on price.
CTAS: Rents and launders work uniforms and supplies mats, first aid and fire protection to businesses on route-based contracts; density of the routes is the moat.
ELV: Sells health insurance as the Blue Cross licensee in fourteen states, plus the Carelon services arm; membership mix between commercial and Medicaid drives the margin.
AMT: REIT owning cell towers in the US and internationally, leasing space on them to carriers on long escalating contracts; adding a second tenant to a tower is nearly pure profit.
ROST: Sells branded apparel and home goods at closeout prices through Ross and dd's Discounts, buying opportunistically in the same way as TJX.
REGN: Sells Eylea for retinal disease and, with Sanofi, Dupixent; the antibody discovery platform is what has produced both and is meant to produce the next.
SKHY: Makes DRAM and NAND flash memory, and is the leading supplier of the high-bandwidth memory stacked beside Nvidia's AI accelerators — which is what separates its cycle from Micron's.
SHEL: Produces oil and gas, runs the largest LNG trading book of any major, refines and markets fuels, and sells power; trading is a real earnings source, not an adjunct.
ARM: Licenses the CPU instruction set and core designs that nearly every phone chip is built on, earning an upfront licence fee plus a royalty on each chip shipped. It fabricates nothing.
BHP: Mines iron ore in Australia, copper in Chile and Australia, and metallurgical coal; iron ore sold to Chinese steel mills still sets the earnings.
SMFG: Japanese banking group: domestic corporate and retail lending, leasing, and a securities arm, with a large overseas loan book.
UL: Sells Dove, Knorr, Hellmann's and Magnum through retailers worldwide, with emerging markets over half of sales; the ice cream business is being separated.
SONY: Sells PlayStation consoles, games and network subscriptions, the image sensors in most phone cameras, and music and film catalogues — plus an insurance arm in Japan.
PDD: Runs Pinduoduo, the discount marketplace in China, and Temu internationally, taking advertising and transaction fees from merchants who ship directly to buyers.
GSK: Sells vaccines including Shingrix, HIV medicines through ViiV, and respiratory and oncology drugs; the consumer brands were spun off as Haleon.
LYG: UK retail bank, the largest mortgage lender in the country, with earnings driven by the deposit margin and by UK house prices rather than by investment banking.
NTES: Develops and operates online games in China, its own and Blizzard titles under licence, plus a music streaming service and an online education arm.
MDLZ: Sells Oreo, Cadbury, Milka and Ritz through retailers worldwide, with emerging markets close to half of revenue; cocoa cost is the swing factor in the margin.
SU: Canadian integrated producer: oil sands mining and upgrading feeding its own refineries and the Petro-Canada retail network, which cushions it against the crude differential.
NGG: Owns and operates the electricity transmission network in England and Wales and gas and power networks in New York and New England — a regulated return on a growing asset base.
CP: Runs the only railroad reaching from Canada through the US to Mexico after the Kansas City Southern merger, hauling grain, intermodal, potash and autos.
BAM: The asset management arm of Brookfield, raising and managing infrastructure, renewable, real estate and credit funds for institutions and earning fees rather than holding the assets.
EOG: Shale producer in the Permian, Eagle Ford and Delaware basins, run on a returns-first drilling model rather than on production growth.
ASX: Packages and tests chips for fabless designers and foundries — the assembly step after the wafer — and is the largest independent provider of it.
ECL: Sells cleaning and water treatment chemicals with the service to run them to restaurants, hotels, hospitals and food plants; the service contract is what makes it recurring.
TRV: Underwrites US commercial and personal property and casualty insurance, earning from underwriting margin and from investing the premium float.
GM: Builds and sells trucks and SUVs in North America, where full-size pickups carry most of the profit, plus GM Financial and the Cruise autonomy programme.
NWG: UK retail and commercial bank, formerly Royal Bank of Scotland, with earnings driven by the deposit margin and UK mortgage competition.
NOC: Builds the B-21 bomber, Sentinel ICBM, space systems and defence electronics for the Pentagon; the programmes are long, sole-source and hard to displace.
HON: Sells aerospace avionics and engines, building automation, industrial automation and advanced materials — four largely unrelated franchises under one balance sheet.
CNI: Runs the Canadian railroad reaching three coasts, hauling grain, forest products, intermodal and petrochemicals; the only North American railroad with Atlantic, Pacific and Gulf access.
AON: Brokes insurance and reinsurance for corporate clients and sells retirement and health benefits consulting; commission and fee income with no underwriting risk.
AMX: Latin America's largest mobile operator, dominant in Mexico and present across the region, plus fixed broadband and pay television.
NSC: Runs the freight railroad across the eastern US in a duopoly with CSX, hauling intermodal, coal, chemicals and autos.
SPG: REIT owning the largest US portfolio of malls and premium outlets, leasing to retailers on long escalating leases with a share of tenant sales.
MFC: Canadian insurer earning a growing share of profit from Asian life insurance and from the Global Wealth and Asset Management arm rather than from the domestic book.
ORLY: Sells car parts through its own stores, weighted to professional mechanics; the distribution network that puts a part within hours of any shop is the moat.
CI: Runs Evernorth, one of the three large pharmacy benefit managers, alongside a commercial health insurance business — the PBM is now the larger half.
AEM: Mines gold in Canada, Finland, Mexico and Australia, with reserves concentrated in politically stable jurisdictions, which is what it charges a premium for.
SLB: Sells drilling, well completion and reservoir services to oil producers worldwide; the largest oilfield services company and the most international.
CL: Sells Colgate toothpaste, Palmolive and Hill's pet food through retailers, with over half of revenue from emerging markets and a dominant global share in toothpaste.
FDX: Delivers express and ground parcels and less-than-truckload freight, running its own aircraft fleet; a fixed-cost network mid-way through merging its express and ground operations.
APO: Manages private equity and credit funds and owns Athene, the annuity writer whose balance sheet supplies the permanent capital the credit business invests.
MSI: Sells the land mobile radio networks police and fire services run on, plus video surveillance and command software; the installed base makes replacement rare and service revenue steady.
HLT: Franchises and manages hotels under Hilton, Hampton, DoubleTree and Waldorf Astoria, collecting fees on room revenue rather than owning the buildings.
KMI: Owns the largest US natural gas pipeline network, moving roughly 40% of the gas consumed in the country under fee-based contracts rather than on the commodity price.
DLR: REIT owning data centres leased to cloud operators and enterprises; the constraint on growth is now grid power, not land or capital.
TRP: Owns the Canadian mainline gas system, the Coastal GasLink pipeline to the LNG terminal, and power assets; contracted tolls rather than commodity exposure.
TDG: Makes proprietary, sole-source aircraft components with no substitute, and prices the aftermarket accordingly — the reason its margins look nothing like an aerospace supplier's.
MPWR: Makes power management chips for data-centre servers, cars and industrial equipment, competing on power density in the voltage regulation feeding AI accelerators.
PCAR: Builds Kenworth, Peterbilt and DAF heavy trucks and sells the parts and financing behind them; the parts business is what carries it through the truck cycle's troughs.
AEP: Regulated electric utility across eleven states with the largest transmission network in the US, spending heavily to connect new data-centre load.
BSX: Sells cardiac rhythm devices, electrophysiology catheters, stents and endoscopy tools to hospitals, with the Farapulse ablation system driving the recent growth.
DB: German universal bank: corporate banking and a fixed income trading franchise, plus asset management through DWS and a domestic retail bank.
CVNA: Sells used cars online, buying, reconditioning and delivering them itself and financing the purchase; a capital-heavy model whose profitability depends on the finance income.
ALL: Underwrites US car and home insurance direct and through agents, having shifted the mix toward direct after re-pricing the auto book.
URI: Rents construction and industrial equipment across North America; scale of the fleet and branch density is what lets it serve national contractors.
WBD: Runs HBO Max, the Warner Bros. studios and the cable networks including CNN and Discovery; the studio and streaming half is being separated from the declining cable half.
APD: Sells industrial gases — hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen — on long on-site contracts to refiners and chemical plants, with large hydrogen projects the current capital commitment.
TGT: Sells general merchandise and groceries through its own stores, competing on private-label brands and store experience rather than on price against Walmart.
GWW: Distributes maintenance and repair supplies to businesses and institutions, holding the inventory that customers need immediately and charging for the availability.
AFL: Sells supplemental health and life insurance, earning most of its profit in Japan, where it is the leading writer of cancer and medical cover.
RSG: Collects and disposes of waste across the US, second in scale to Waste Management and owning the landfills that give it the same pricing power.
RELX: Sells scientific journals through Elsevier, legal research through LexisNexis, and risk and analytics data to insurers and banks — subscription revenue with very high renewal.
TFC: US regional bank formed from the BB&T and SunTrust merger, doing retail and commercial banking across the southeast, plus an insurance brokerage.
VALE: Mines iron ore in Brazil at among the lowest costs in the world, plus nickel and copper; earnings track the iron ore price sold into China.
AJG: Brokes insurance for mid-market companies and does claims administration; grows by acquiring smaller brokers, which is the model as much as the organic business is.
CRH: Sells aggregates, cement and asphalt and does the road paving with them, mostly in the US, where public infrastructure spending is the demand driver.
HPE: Sells servers, storage and networking to enterprises, with AI servers and the Juniper networking acquisition the current growth, and GreenLake the subscription push.
IMO: Canadian integrated producer majority-owned by ExxonMobil: oil sands production, refining and the Esso retail network.
NKE: Designs and sells athletic footwear and apparel made by contract manufacturers in Asia, shifting sales toward its own stores and app and away from wholesale.
MET: Sells group life, dental and disability insurance to employers, plus retirement and annuity products; earnings depend on the investment yield on a very large fixed income portfolio.
B: Mines gold and copper across Africa, the Americas and Papua New Guinea, holding tier-one deposits alongside the jurisdictional risk that comes with several of them.
FIX: Installs and services the mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems inside commercial buildings, with data centres now the fastest-growing end market in its backlog.
D: Regulated electric utility serving Virginia, where the density of data centres in Loudoun County has made load growth the central planning problem.
BE: Sells solid-oxide fuel cells that generate power on site from natural gas or hydrogen, sold to data centres and industrial customers waiting for a grid connection.
COR: Distributes prescription drugs from manufacturers to pharmacies and hospitals at very thin margins on very large volume, plus specialty and oncology services.
BKR: Sells oilfield equipment and services, and separately the gas turbines and compressors that LNG plants are built around — the second half is the growth.
O: REIT owning freestanding retail properties let to a single tenant on long triple-net leases, paying its dividend monthly, which is most of its retail following.
TEL: Makes connectors and sensors for cars, aircraft, factories and data centres; the content per electric vehicle is materially higher than per combustion one.
NUE: Melts scrap in electric arc furnaces to make steel, a lower-cost and less capital-intensive process than a blast furnace, and sells joists, decking and rebar downstream.
TRGP: Gathers, processes and transports natural gas liquids from the Permian to the Gulf Coast for export; fee-based on volume with some commodity exposure.
SRE: Utility holding company owning San Diego Gas & Electric, the Texas transmission utility Oncor, and LNG export terminals on the Gulf Coast.
NXPI: Makes chips for cars — radar, in-vehicle networking, battery management — and for secure identification and payment; automotive is over half of revenue.
DAL: Runs the US airline with the strongest premium cabin and loyalty economics, where the American Express co-brand contributes a large and steadier share of profit than seats do.
F: Builds and sells trucks and SUVs, with the F-Series the profit centre, plus Ford Credit and a loss-making electric vehicle unit being retrenched.
OKE: Owns natural gas gathering, processing and NGL pipelines from the Bakken and Permian to the Gulf, earning fees on volume rather than on price.
FANG: Permian shale producer with the lowest cost structure among the pure plays, having consolidated acreage rather than expanded into other basins.
PSA: REIT owning self-storage facilities across the US; occupancy and the ability to raise rents on existing tenants matter more than new development.
OXY: Produces oil and gas in the Permian and Middle East, owns a chemicals business, and is building direct air capture plants — the last funded partly by policy credits.
CVE: Canadian integrated producer: oil sands production feeding refineries it part-owns in the US Midwest, which hedges the heavy crude differential.
LITE: Makes the optical components and lasers that carry traffic between AI accelerators and between data centres; demand now tracks cloud capital spending rather than telecom.
LNG: Owns and operates the Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi LNG export terminals, selling liquefaction capacity on twenty-year take-or-pay contracts rather than selling gas.
FAST: Distributes fasteners and industrial supplies through branches and vending machines placed inside customers' own plants, which is what makes the relationship hard to displace.
KEYS: Sells the test and measurement instruments used to design and validate chips, wireless networks and cars; sold into engineering budgets rather than production ones.
CAH: Distributes prescription drugs to pharmacies and hospitals, and manufactures its own medical and surgical products — the third of the big three US drug distributors.
ROK: Sells factory automation — programmable controllers, drives, industrial software — to manufacturers, with the installed base and the engineers trained on it the switching cost.
